La peste noire atteint l'Europe par la C: The Black Death reached Europe through Crimea and Sicily in 1347. Within a few years, it killed 30 to 60% of Europeans, depending on the estimates. Doctors blamed miasmas and the stars; Jews were accused of poisoning wells and massacred, in Strasbourg and elsewhere. Lacking a cause, people found a culprit. Ragusa, today's Dubrovnik, imposed thirty days of isolation on arrivals in 1377; Venice went to 40 days in 1448: the quarantine. The plague bacillus was only identified in 1894, by Alexandre Yersin.

En 424 av. J.-C., le général spartiate B: In 424 BC, the Spartan general Brasidas takes Amphipolis and offers mild terms. The cities allied to Athens hear of it and secretly call him in, each wanting to be the first to revolt. They misjudged Athens's power, notes Thucydides: it is the habit of mankind to entrust to careless hope what they long for, and to use reason to thrust aside what they do not fancy. Today we call it wishful thinking.

Dans les Réfutations sophistiques, Arist: In the Sophistical Refutations, Aristotle draws up the first catalogue of misleading reasoning: thirteen fallacies. Six depend on words, like equivocation, when the same word changes meaning along the way. Seven do not: begging the question, which assumes what had to be proved, false cause, or the many-questions fallacy, which hides several questions in one. Twenty-three centuries later, critical thinking manuals still copy them.
Treize façons de mal raisonner, répertor: Thirteen ways to reason badly, catalogued twenty-three centuries ago. Have you found a fourteenth?
En 1620, Francis Bacon publie le Novum O: In 1620, Francis Bacon publishes the Novum Organum and lists the idols that lead the mind astray: those of the tribe, the cave, the marketplace and the theatre. He tells how a man was shown, in a temple, the pictures offered by those who had made a vow and escaped shipwreck, to convince him of the gods' power. He asked: "But where are they painted that were drowned after their vows?"
On ne compte que les rescapés. Les noyés: We only count the survivors. The drowned don't leave five-star reviews.
En 1713, Nicolas Bernoulli imagine un je: In 1713, Nicolaus Bernoulli devises a strange game. In its now classic version, a coin is tossed until it lands heads, and the prize doubles with each toss. The expected prize is infinite, and yet nobody would pay much to play. In 1738, his cousin Daniel Bernoulli publishes an explanation with the St. Petersburg Academy: the value of a gain does not grow like the sum, but like its logarithm.
Un gain infini, et personne ne veut joue: An infinite prize, and nobody wants to play. Humans are sometimes wiser than their sums. Rarely.
En 1841, le journaliste écossais Charles: In 1841, the Scottish journalist Charles Mackay publishes a book on the madness of crowds. He tells of the Dutch tulip mania of 1636-1637: bulbs sold for fortunes, then the crash, and a sailor thrown in jail for eating a bulb he took for an onion. The historian Anne Goldgar, digging through the archives, found a much smaller episode: few people involved, and no bankruptcy to be found. The madness was partly in the telling.
A crash that mostly ruined the stories. You, on the other hand, really do lose two squares.
À une foire aux bestiaux de Plymouth, de: At a livestock fair in Plymouth, visitors bet on the weight of an ox once slaughtered and dressed. Francis Galton collects the 787 legible tickets. In 1907, in the journal Nature, he publishes the result: the median estimate, 1,207 pounds, is only 9 pounds off the announced real weight, 1,198. The mean, published later, is even closer. Taken together, the crowd had got it right.
Huit cents personnes ensemble ont deviné: Eight hundred people together guessed an ox's weight. You alone, I'm not so sure.
En 1951, le psychologue Solomon Asch mon: In 1951, the psychologist Solomon Asch shows students three lines and asks which one is the same length as a reference line. It is easy: alone, they are wrong less than once in a hundred. But in the group, seven accomplices first give the same wrong answer out loud. Result: about a third of the answers follow the majority, and three participants out of four give in at least once.
Sept personnes se trompent à voix haute: Seven people are wrong out loud and you follow them. Lucky that I'm the only one talking to you.
En 1951, Edward Simpson, ancien décrypte: In 1951, Edward Simpson, a former Bletchley Park codebreaker, describes a trap in statistical tables: a trend visible in every group can reverse when the groups are added together. The famous example comes from Berkeley, in 1973: 44% of male applicants are admitted, against 35% of women. Yet, department by department, most admit women slightly more. Women mostly applied where rejection rates were highest.
Additionner deux bonnes nouvelles peut d: Adding two pieces of good news can give bad news. Like your last two answers.
En 1960, le psychologue Peter Wason donn: In 1960, the psychologist Peter Wason gives his subjects the sequence 2, 4, 6 and asks them to find the rule by proposing other sets of three numbers. Most imagine a rule that is too specific, such as "add 2", and only propose sequences that confirm it: 8, 10, 12. They announce their rule, confident, and are wrong. The real one was much simpler: any ascending sequence. To find it, you had to try to prove yourself wrong.

En 1974, Amos Tversky et Daniel Kahneman: In 1974, Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman spin a rigged wheel in front of their subjects that stops on 10 or on 65. Then they ask: what percentage of UN countries are African? Those who saw 10 typically answer 25%; those who saw 65, 45%. A number drawn at random, with nothing to do with the question, pulled the answers towards it. This is the anchoring effect.
Un chiffre au hasard a suffi à les influ: A random number was enough to sway them. So remember this one: a 100% chance you'll study tonight.
En 1974, Elizabeth Loftus et John Palmer: In 1974, Elizabeth Loftus and John Palmer show a film of a car accident, then ask how fast the cars were going when they hit, or smashed into, each other. With "smashed", the estimates go up: 40.8 against 34 miles per hour. A week later, 16 people out of 50 in the "smashed" group remember broken glass, against 7 in the other group. The film showed none.
Un seul mot a fabriqué un souvenir. Pens: A single word manufactured a memory. Think of it next time you're sure you've already studied.
En 1978, Sarah Lichtenstein, Paul Slovic: In 1978, Sarah Lichtenstein, Paul Slovic, Baruch Fischhoff and their colleagues ask Americans to estimate the number of deaths caused by a whole range of hazards. Subjects overestimate rare causes and underestimate frequent ones. They judge accidents almost as deadly as diseases, which in fact kill about sixteen times more. They believe homicide is more frequent than suicide, which is actually twice as frequent. What gets talked about comes to mind faster.
Ce qui fait la une n'est pas ce qui tue: What makes the headlines isn't what kills the most. Nor is what loses you points.

In it he offers a baloney detection kit: have facts confirmed by independent sources, consider several hypotheses, prefer the simplest, check that a claim can be refuted. And he tells the story of a dragon in his garage: invisible, floating, breathing heatless fire. Impossible to prove it does not exist. But what is the difference from no dragon at all?

En 1995, à Pittsburgh, McArthur Wheeler: In 1995, in Pittsburgh, McArthur Wheeler robs two banks with his face uncovered. Arrested that same evening, he is surprised: he had rubbed lemon juice on his face, supposed to make him invisible to cameras. David Dunning and Justin Kruger's 1999 paper opens with this story. The weakest participants on their logic test, on average at the 12th percentile, rated themselves at the 62nd. To see that you are bad, you need the very skill you lack.

En janvier 2013, le programmeur italien: In January 2013, the Italian programmer Alberto Brandolini states a law: the energy needed to refute bullshit is an order of magnitude bigger than that needed to produce it. He had just read Daniel Kahneman's book on the two systems of thought and watched a TV debate with Silvio Berlusconi. The idea is old: in 1710, Jonathan Swift was already writing that falsehood flies and truth comes limping after it.
Réfuter une bêtise coûte dix fois plus q: Refuting nonsense costs ten times more than saying it. That's why I correct you so often: I'm very invested.
En 1948, le psychologue américain Bertra: In 1948, the American psychologist Bertram Forer gives a personality test to 39 students, then hands each a "personalised" profile. In fact they all receive the same text, copied from an astrology book bought at a newsstand. The students rate their profile as accurate at 4.3 out of 5. Vague, flattering sentences presented as made for us are enough: this is the Barnum effect, as Paul Meehl named it in 1956. Psychics and horoscopes live off it.
Vous êtes curieux, parfois indécis, et v: You are curious, sometimes indecisive, and have untapped potential. Sounds like you? Step back two spaces.

Entre 1011 et 1021, Ibn al-Haytham, que: Between 1011 and 1021, Ibn al-Haytham, whom the West would call Alhazen, wrote his Book of Optics, in seven volumes. Euclid and Ptolemy believed that the eye sends out rays toward things. He argued the opposite: light leaves objects, travels in straight lines and enters the eye. He relied on experiments rather than on the authority of the ancients, and described the camera obscura, where a small hole projects an image. Translated into Latin around 1200, his book would feed European optics until the 17th century.
